title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: A Will, A Death, A Question

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close reading of one of Dickens's most ambitious, most underrated, and in many ways most modern novels.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be moving through the whole of Our Mutual Friend — chapter by chapter, character by character, dustheap by dustheap.
This is a novel about money, identity, death, and resurrection — and Dickens builds it from the very first page with a corpse dragged from the Thames and a fortune nobody can quite claim.
Joining me today are three readers who each bring something irreplaceable to this conversation.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — she wants to know exactly how it ticks.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian whose work asks who benefits and who suffers from the way society organises itself — and Dickens gives him enormous material to work with.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since she was a teenager — she reads it for what it feels like, what makes you stop mid-page and simply breathe.
We begin where Dickens begins — with a will, a death, and a question that drives the whole machinery of the plot.

Old John Harmon, a dust contractor of legendary miserliness, has died and left behind a fortune accumulated from London's filth — and a will with a condition attached that will pull every character in the novel into its orbit.
Eleanor, let me start with you — what does Dickens actually do in these opening chapters that is so distinctive?
What strikes me every time I return to the opening is how aggressively Dickens refuses to orient the reader.
We begin on the river at night — Gaffer Hexam and his daughter Lizzie pulling something through the dark water — and we are given no context, no backstory, no reassuring narrative hand-holding.
Dickens opens with a scene of scavenging that is frankly grotesque, and he trusts us to stay with the discomfort.
And then — almost immediately — we cut to a dinner party in the Veneerings' ostentatious home, which is as polished and hollow as the riverbank was raw.
That juxtaposition — the body in the river and the dinner table — is announced right at the start as the novel's governing structural principle.
Dickens is telling us: everything in this world connects, and nothing connects comfortably.
I'd push that further, because what Dickens is doing structurally he is also doing politically.
The Veneerings — that name is barely even a metaphor, it's a direct statement — they have made themselves out of money so new it hasn't dried.
And the guests at that table — Twemlow, Podsnap, the Lammles — are all there to perform society for one another.
What Dickens captures is a world in which social position is pure performance, pure surface — and he says so in the very word he chooses for the family name.
Meanwhile, the actual production of wealth — the dustheaps, the river, the labour — is happening elsewhere, among people who don't get invited to those dinners.
That's not accidental. That is the system working exactly as designed.
What I keep thinking about is the will itself — because it's such a strange, almost cruel dramatic engine.
Old Harmon has essentially bought his son a wife from beyond the grave.
John Harmon junior must marry Bella Wilfer — a girl he has never met — or the fortune passes entirely to the Boffins.
And then the young man who is supposed to come home and claim both the fortune and the bride — turns up dead in the Thames.
Or does he?
That question — that suspended, unverified death — is what gives the whole novel its particular atmosphere of instability.
Nobody in this novel is entirely who they say they are, and it starts right here, with an identity that may or may not be a corpse.
Caroline has put her finger on something technically brilliant — Dickens gives us a mystery plot, but the mystery isn't whodunit, it's who IS he.
And the genius is that we the readers know fairly early that John Harmon is alive and moving through the novel in disguise as John Rokesmith.
Dickens doesn't withhold the secret from us — he withholds it from the other characters.
Which means the dramatic irony is incredibly productive — we watch Bella Wilfer gradually fall in love with the man she was meant to marry, not knowing he is that man.
It's a masterclass in what you might call ironic intimacy — the reader is always two steps ahead, and that gap is where the emotion lives.
I want to come back to what that will actually represents as a social document.
Old Harmon made his money from dust — from the refuse of the city — which is to say, from the labour of people sifting and sorting London's waste.
And rather than dissolving that wealth, redistributing it, letting it do anything generous in the world — he locks it up in a condition of patriarchal control.
The will is the legal instrument through which a dead miser continues to dominate the living.
That's Dickens at his most clear-eyed about property and inheritance — institutions that launder power across generations and call it natural.
And that sense of wealth as something simultaneously filthy and irresistible runs right through the novel — we'll be returning to the dustheaps and everything they symbolise as the series continues.
But before we go further into the novel's machinery, I want to ask each of you something more personal.
This novel has a reputation for being daunting — long, densely plotted, with a cast of dozens.
Caroline — for someone coming to it for the first time, what is the one thing you would tell them to hold onto in these opening chapters?
The river.
The Thames in this novel is not scenery — it is a character, and it has moods and a memory and it takes things and gives them back changed.
When Dickens describes Gaffer Hexam on the water in that first chapter — the way the body he's towing barely disturbs the surface — there's a terrible poetry to it.
The river connects every level of this society — the Hexams at the bottom, the Veneerings at the top — and it doesn't care about any of them.
If you hold onto the river, you hold onto the novel's heartbeat.
The river as heartbeat — that's a beautiful way to put it, and a perfect place to pause before we go deeper.
In our next segment, we'll begin reading closely — the opening chapters, the Thames at night, and the first great question this novel asks us to sit with.
Stay with us.
Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — and rewards the attention.
I'm your host, and today we are going deep into the novel's central obsession: money.
Not money as a background condition, but money as architecture — the material from which every relationship, every ambition, every self in this novel is constructed.
To help me think through what Dickens is actually doing, I have three extraordinary readers with me.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who cares passionately about how effects are made — the craft beneath the surface.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads novels as anatomies of class power, and he is going to have a great deal to say about this particular novel.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has re-read Our Mutual Friend many times and brings a reader's hard-won intimacy with the text.
Our subject today is what I'm calling the architecture of greed — the way the novel builds its entire world out of the pursuit of inherited wealth.
The Harmon dust-mounds, the Veneering dinner table, the river itself — all of it is greed given physical form.
Eleanor, let's start with you — because I think Dickens announces this theme in an almost architectural way in the very opening pages.
He does, and the audacity of it is still startling when you go back to it.
The novel opens not with a character we're invited to sympathise with, but with Gaffer Hexam on the Thames, towing a corpse for its pocket contents.
Dickens frames this as an economy in miniature — the dead are worth more to Gaffer than the living, because the dead can be robbed without complaint.
What Dickens is building from page one is a world where value is extracted from bodies — literally.
And then he widens the lens to the Veneerings' dinner party, and we realise the extraction is just as total up the social scale — it's merely better dressed.
There's a passage early on where Dickens describes the Veneerings' dining table and their guests with this magnificent savagery.
He writes of them: 'Mr and Mrs Veneering were bran-new people in a bran-new house in a bran-new quarter of London.'
That triple repetition of 'bran-new' is doing so much work — it's satirical but it's also structurally precise.
Everything about the Veneerings is surface — and Dickens tells you this in the rhythm of the sentence before you've even processed the content.
And that surface is doing ideological work, which I think Dickens understood more clearly than he's sometimes given credit for.
The Veneerings are not just comic grotesques — they are a diagnosis of how capital reproduces social legitimacy.
You buy the house, you buy the plate, you buy the guests — and within one dinner party you have purchased the fiction of belonging.
But the more radical architecture in the novel, to my mind, is the dust-mound inheritance itself.
Old Harmon has built a fortune out of the city's refuse — literally the waste that polite society generates and then refuses to see.
Dickens is making a pun, and it is one of the most precise puns in English literature: the Harmon fortune is refuse and it is what the respectable refuse to acknowledge.
Dickens describes old Harmon as 'the Dust Contractor' and his wealth as accumulated from 'dust, ashes, and such like.'
'Dust, ashes, and such like' — that 'such like' is devastating in its vagueness, because it means everything the respectable world excretes and denies.
The entire plot — who gets the money, who marries whom, who transforms themselves for the inheritance — is constructed on top of that mound of filth.
Dickens is telling us, with perfect structural clarity, that Victorian society's foundations are not moral — they are excremental.
What strikes me, re-reading this, is how funny it is alongside how dark it is — Dickens holds those two things in an almost impossible balance.
The Veneering chapters, for me, have always been the most dazzlingly comic sections of the novel.
The device of the Analytical — the Veneerings' butler, who silently registers contempt for everything — is a small masterpiece of satire.
He moves around the table dispensing wine and disapproval in equal measure, and Dickens never lets him speak — his silence is louder than any speech.
But what gets me is the moment when Dickens describes the mirror above the Veneerings' sideboard — which reflects all their guests.
He calls it 'the great looking-glass above the sideboard' and says it reflects 'the table and company, and the Analytical Chemist — .'
That mirror is the novel in miniature — a surface that shows us everyone performing for one another, everyone watched and watching.
And it is made, of course, of the Veneering silver — which is new, which is bought, which reflects back only what money can assemble.
Caroline's point about the mirror goes to something I find technically fascinating — Dickens's use of the Veneerings as a satirical frame through which we keep viewing the novel's other plots.
They are not protagonists. They are the context — the ambient moral weather of the world John Harmon returns to.
And structurally, Dickens keeps returning to their dinner table the way a playwright returns to a single stage set — to show us time passing, society not changing.
The genius of Bella Wilfer's arc is that she begins as someone who openly, honestly admits she wants money — which is, in this world, practically radical.
She says something to the effect that she has made up her mind to be rich — she is mercenary and she knows it.
'I am mercenary, and I am always to be found when money's concerned' — she says it with a kind of fierce self-awareness that almost everyone else in the novel lacks.
The Veneerings will never say that. Podsnap will never say that. Bella says it, and her honesty is a structural counterweight to the novel's pervasive hypocrisy.
Bella's honesty is important but I want to push back slightly, because I think the novel ultimately domesticates her.
Her education is precisely a process of learning to not want money — or rather, to want it in the approved, feminine, subordinated way.
John Rokesmith — who is of course Harmon in disguise — tests her precisely by making her live without wealth first.
And she passes the test by becoming domestic, small, content — which the novel rewards by then giving her the fortune anyway.
The architecture of greed in Our Mutual Friend is deeply gendered — men pursue wealth openly; women are educated out of the desire and then wealth descends upon them.
Podsnap's great declaration that something is 'Not English' whenever it challenges his comfort is the male version of this — the refusal to see what the system is built on.
He is the Analytical made loud — the same contempt, but expressed as power rather than silence.
That comparison between Podsnap and the Analytical is something I will be thinking about for a while.
But I want to come back to the mounds, because I think we haven't quite honoured how strange and wonderful they are as objects in the novel.
They loom over Boffin's Bower — they are literally present on the horizon.
And Noddy Boffin, the Golden Dustman, carries the mounds with him as a kind of moral history — he is kind precisely because he has not forgotten what wealth is made of.
There is that gorgeous passage where Dickens describes Boffin coming into his inheritance — with the mounds as his backdrop.
He describes Boffin as 'a broad, round-shouldered, one-sided old fellow in mourning, coming comically ambling' — and that ambling is everything.
It is not a triumphant entrance — it is a shuffle, a man who doesn't quite know what to do with what has been thrust upon him.
Boffin is the novel's proof that money doesn't have to corrupt — but also that the pressure it exerts on everyone around you is nearly irresistible.
The Boffin arc is, I think, one of the most contentious structural decisions in the novel — and I find it defensible precisely because of what Caroline describes.
When Boffin appears to succumb to avarice — collecting misers, becoming harsh, turning on Rokesmith — many readers feel betrayed.
But Dickens is playing a long game: the apparent corruption is a performance, staged to educate Bella.
The question is whether the performance is too convincing — whether Dickens has accidentally written genuine avarice.
Silas Wegg circling the mounds with his wooden leg and his eyes full of scheming — that is a darker, truer portrait of what the mounds do to people.
Wegg is the figure in whom greed is most fully, most grotesquely anatomised — every page he appears on, the prose gets sharper and more savage.
Wegg is essential to this discussion and I'm glad Eleanor raised him.
He is a man with no capital — literally a street vendor of fruit and literature — who believes the mounds owe him something.
His conviction that a will exists that would give him the fortune is not simply greed — it is the aspiration of the dispossessed, corrupted into paranoia.
The system has taught Wegg that the only route out of poverty is a windfall — because there is no other route available to him.
So his villainy — real, comic, grotesque as it is — is also the system's product.
When Wegg recites poetry to Boffin for wages and then schemes to blackmail him, the distance between those two acts is not as great as it looks.
Both are attempts by a man with nothing to extract something from a man with everything — which is, in miniature, the logic of the whole novel.
That is a remarkable formulation — Wegg as the novel's logic made explicit.
And it brings us naturally to a question I want to put to all three of you before we move on: does this novel believe there is any escape from that logic?
Is there any character who genuinely stands outside the architecture of greed — or is everyone, at some level, contaminated?
Lizzie Hexam.
She is the character who, for me, most completely refuses the novel's economy — not because she is above desire, but because she is inside a different set of values entirely.
She grew up on the river taking money from the dead alongside her father — and she loathes it.
Her entire arc is a flight from that inheritance — not towards money, but towards something the novel can barely name.
Eugene Wrayburn sees it in her — that's what draws him, and it's what finally changes him.
I'd add Eugene himself — but only after he almost dies.
The near-drowning is structurally a rebirth — Dickens is quite literal about that — and what Eugene is reborn into is a self that doesn't need social approval to validate its choices.
He marries Lizzie against everything his class demands — and the novel, unusually for Dickens, refuses to punish him for it.
The deathbed scene where he insists on marrying her — where Mortimer watches — is one of the most quietly radical moments in Victorian fiction.
I'll offer a more sceptical answer: I think the novel's true escapees are the ones it can barely integrate — Mr. Venus, for instance, in his small way.
But more seriously: Riah, the Jewish money-lender who is forced to appear rapacious on behalf of Fledgeby — and knows it.
Riah is the most structurally lucid character in the book because he is made to embody the greed of others — he is the face of a system that hides its actual face.
He knows exactly what the architecture of greed is, because he is its instrument and its victim simultaneously.
Riah as the novel's most lucid observer — I find that a genuinely arresting way of putting it.
We're going to stay with this question of who the novel sees clearly and who it doesn't when we turn next to the river — and what it carries.
Thank you Eleanor, Daniel, Caroline — stay with us.

segments.title: Money's Music: Reading the Language of Exchange

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take one of the most extraordinary novels in the English language and give it the close attention it deserves.
Our Mutual Friend is Dickens at his most ambitious — a novel obsessed with money, with what money does to people, and with the strange language that grows up around it.
Today's segment is called Money's Music — because in this novel, exchange has its own vocabulary, its own rhythms, its own dark poetry.
I'm joined by three wonderful readers who each bring something distinct to the table.
Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose particular gift is the architecture of sentences — she can hear Dickens thinking, as she puts it.
Daniel Rosen reads novels as anatomies of class power — he's the person who asks who is actually paying for all this, and who is suffering.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite got over it — in the best possible way.
Eleanor, let's start with you — because the language of money in this novel is something you've written about with real precision.
The first thing I want to say is that Dickens never lets money be abstract in this novel.
Every transaction has a texture — a smell, almost.
Think about the Veneerings' dinner table — it's introduced to us as if it were a financial prospectus.
The furniture is new, the silver is new, the guests are new — everything is recent acquisition performing as established wealth.
Dickens describes the great looking-glass above the sideboard as reflecting the table and company, and he calls it the Analytical Chemist.
"The great looking-glass above the sideboard reflects the table and the company. Reflects the new Veneering crest, in gold and eke in silver, frosted and also thawed, a camel of all work."
That word 'new' is doing relentless work — Dickens hammers it like a coin being struck.
The whole scene is structured as a ledger — item by item, acquisition by acquisition — and that structural choice is itself a satirical act.
Eleanor is right that the structure is a ledger — and I'd press that point further.
The Veneerings don't just have new money — they are new money, indistinguishable from the objects they own.
What Dickens is diagnosing here is commodity fetishism decades before Marx named it — the way capital turns persons into things and things into persons.
And the dust mounds — Harmon's dust mounds — are the novel's great emblem of this inversion.
Waste becomes wealth. Filth becomes inheritance. The ground of the plot is literally the accumulated refuse of a society.
Dickens gives Boffin a line early on that cuts to the heart of it — when he's asked about the dust, he says something to the effect that money is the root of all evil, and the root of all the dust.
The joke is that Boffin can't separate virtue from finance — and neither, Dickens suggests, can his society.
What moves me about the dust mounds is how tactile they are — you feel their weight, their smell, their ugliness.
And yet Boffin — the Golden Dustman — is one of the warmest presences in the book.
Dickens gives us this wonderful comedy in which Boffin pretends to be corrupted by his sudden wealth — he hires Silas Wegg to read to him about misers.
And the language of those scenes — Wegg performing Decline and Fall at that dusty bower — is gloriously absurd.
There's a phrase I keep coming back to — when Boffin first takes possession of the house and Dickens writes of him as a man who has come into his property 'staring' at it.
It's such a small verb but it carries everything — the bewilderment, the pride, the slight terror of sudden wealth.
Dickens is listening to what money sounds like when it first lands in the hands of someone who didn't expect it.
Caroline's point about sound is exactly where I want to go next — because the language of exchange in this novel is not only visual, it's auditory.
Consider the Lammles' courtship — two fortune-hunters who discover on their wedding morning that each has deceived the other.
Dickens renders that conversation on the beach with a kind of cold musical precision — the words are formal but the underneath is fury.
He writes of them as reaching an understanding — and the word 'understanding' is doing exquisite ironic work there.
"Mr and Mrs Lammle have agreed to keep up appearances to Society. Mr and Mrs Lammle have agreed to keep up appearances to one another."
The repetition there is devastating — it's a marriage reduced to a business contract, read aloud in parallel clauses like balance-sheet entries.
The music of that sentence is the music of a deal closing — and it's one of the most chilling moments in the novel.
The Lammle scene is the clearest place in the novel where marriage is stripped of all romantic mystification and shown for what it is — a property arrangement.
And notice that they don't separate — they double down, they collaborate.
Because in Dickens's world, two people with nothing are still more powerful as a unit — they can run a longer con together.
This is what the novel understands about capitalism that is genuinely radical — it shows how people internalise market logic so deeply that even their intimate relationships become transactional.
And then set against the Lammles you have Lizzie Hexam — a woman with no capital, no social position — who is the moral centre the novel keeps returning to.
The contrast is not sentimental — it's structural. Lizzie's integrity is precisely defined by what she refuses to trade.
Lizzie is the character I come back to most on every re-reading.
She rows on the river, she reads the fire, she carries her brother's ambitions on her back — and she does it all without self-pity, which makes her heartbreaking.
There's a scene where her father Gaffer Hexam is out on the river at night, towing a drowned body — and Dickens opens the whole novel with it.
He sets up the language of the river as the novel's first economic space — bodies are found, pockets are searched, death is a livelihood.
And little Lizzie is there in the boat — not reading, watching the water, already implicated in the transaction.
Dickens writes of Gaffer that he looked at the bottom of the boat, and he looked at the river — as if they were the same thing.
The river is always an economy in this novel — always a place where things are converted into other things.
The river as economy — I think that's the key to how Dickens builds the whole book architecturally.
Everything flows. Money flows, bodies flow, rumour flows — and Dickens constructs the plot as a kind of circulation system.
John Harmon — or Rokesmith, or Julius Handford, whatever we want to call him at any given moment — is himself a circulating currency.
He's the inheritance that keeps changing hands — the value that the whole novel is organised around, and yet refuses to be pinned down.
That structural choice — the man who fakes his own death to observe how money reshapes the people who stand to inherit it — is a novelist's masterstroke.
Because it lets Dickens run an experiment: remove the heir, watch what the money does.
And what the money does — the novel's answer to Eleanor's experiment — is reveal everyone.
Bella Wilfer is the character I find most interesting in this regard — because she starts the novel as someone who knows her own corruption and admits it without shame.
She tells her father — her dear Pa — that she is mercenary, that she was bequeathed to a dead stranger, and that she hates it, but she wants money all the same.
Dickens gives her a line that has always struck me as extraordinary in its frankness.
"I love money, and want money — want it dreadfully. I hate to be poor, and we are degradingly poor, offensively poor, miserably poor, beastly poor."
The accumulation of adverbs there — degradingly, offensively, miserably, beastly — is Dickens letting Bella's class resentment fully sound.
It's not pretty — but it's honest. And honesty about money is rarer in Victorian fiction than we sometimes pretend.
I love Bella for exactly that — she says the unsayable.
And her scenes with her father Rumty Wilfer — who is this marvellous small downtrodden clerk — have a warmth that acts as a counterweight to all the mercenary scheming.
But what I find wonderful technically is how Dickens modulates Bella's voice as her understanding of money deepens.
By the end, when she has chosen Rokesmith with his apparent poverty, her language about money has become almost tender — she handles the concept differently.
That's Dickens's great trick with her — he runs the education of a mercenary heart, and the music of her sentences changes as she changes.
The music of her sentences changes as she changes — I think that's a wonderful formulation to carry with us into the next part of our discussion.
We've been tracing the language of money from the Veneerings' table to the dust mounds, from the Lammles' cold compact to Bella's naked ambition.
What we've found is that in this novel, the way characters speak about money is the most intimate thing about them.
Coming up, we'll turn to the river itself — and to what floats to the surface when a society built on concealment is asked to give up its dead.

segments.title: Bella at the Mirror: Desire and Becoming

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been tracing the novel's great social comedy — the dust heaps, the nouveaux riches, the river's dark commerce.
But now we turn to something more intimate: the inner life of Bella Wilfer.
Bella is one of Dickens's most psychologically alive creations — a young woman who openly confesses her hunger for money and yet is capable of profound moral transformation.
Our segment title is Bella at the Mirror — and that image of self-scrutiny, of a character watching herself want things, sits at the heart of what makes her so compelling.
Eleanor, you've written about how Dickens constructs desire in this novel — where do you want to begin with Bella?
Bella is extraordinary precisely because Dickens gives her what he almost never gives his young heroines: a frank, unashamed interiority about money.
She announces herself to us very early as a mercenary little wretch — and crucially, those are her own words about herself.

There's a scene in Book One where she tells her father — dear, helpless Pa — something to the effect that she was bequeathed as a legacy to a stranger, and that she finds the whole arrangement degrading.
The point is that she doesn't romanticise her situation. She sees it with cold clarity.
And that mirror quality — watching yourself, naming your own faults aloud — is actually Dickens's most sophisticated psychological technique in this novel.
Because a character who can name her own mercenary nature is already, structurally, on the road to outgrowing it.
I'd push on that a little, Eleanor, because I think we risk sentimentalising Bella's self-knowledge if we read it purely as psychological progress.
Bella's desire for money is not a character flaw floating free of context — it is the entirely rational response of a woman with no economic agency in a society that sells women in marriage markets.
She was literally named in a dead man's will as if she were a piece of property.
So when Bella sits at her metaphorical mirror and calls herself mercenary, she is diagnosing the logic of the system — not merely her own weakness.
Dickens understands this, I think, more clearly than he always gets credit for.

He makes Bella's hunger for gold utterly comprehensible — because he has shown us the Wilfer household, that cramped genteel poverty, Mrs. Wilfer's magnificent wounded dignity masking real destitution.
Both of those things feel true to me, and what I find myself returning to is the texture of those scenes between Bella and her father.
R.W. Wilfer — the Cherub, as Bella calls him — is this gentle, ineffectual, completely loving presence, and their relationship is the warmest thing in Bella's world for much of the novel.
There's that wonderful Greenwich dinner — Bella and Pa having their little holiday feast — which is just suffused with tenderness.
And it matters because it shows us what Bella is actually made of underneath the mercenary declaration.
She is capable of pure, uncalculating affection.
So the transformation the novel charts isn't really from cold to warm — she was always warm.
It's from confusion about what she values to clarity about it.
Caroline, that distinction — confusion to clarity rather than cold to warm — is exactly right, and it's what saves Bella from being a conventional redemption arc.
Dickens is very careful never to make her actually bad. She's never cruel in a damaging way.
The craft choice I find fascinating is how he handles her relationship with John Rokesmith — or rather, with John who she doesn't yet know is John Harmon.
She is drawn to him against her own stated programme of marrying for money.
Her behaviour keeps betraying her philosophy — and Dickens renders that contradiction in the very rhythm of her speech.
She'll say something sharp and materialistic and then immediately do something generous and feeling.
The gap between her self-image and her actions is where the comedy lives — and also where the drama lives.
The Boffin plot is where I think Dickens is simultaneously most radical and most troubling.
Noddy Boffin performs a transformation into a miser — the Golden Dustman becoming a figure of grotesque acquisition — specifically to test Bella and disgust her into rejecting wealth.
On one level this is a beautiful inversion: the man who inherits the dust heap uses the symbolism of hoarded gold to free a young woman from its tyranny.
But there's something uncomfortable in the architecture of it — Bella is being manipulated into her own liberation.
The men around her — Boffin, Harmon, Rokesmith — have all agreed to an experiment in which she is the subject.
However warmly Dickens intends it, that is a patriarchal structure dressed in generous clothing.
That critique lands, Daniel, and I've wrestled with it across multiple re-readings.
But what softens it for me — not excuses it, softens it — is the scene where Bella rejects Boffin's gold in real time, before she knows the truth.
She stands up for John Rokesmith when Boffin dismisses and humiliates him.
And she does it knowing it will cost her the inheritance.
She walks away from the money of her own volition, in ignorance of the whole conspiracy.
So the manipulation, however troubling its architecture, does not actually produce the outcome — her own character does.
And I think that moment is where the mirror image in our title becomes literal.
Bella has been looking at herself throughout the novel — sometimes with vanity, sometimes with wry self-criticism.
Dickens even gives her actual mirror scenes — moments of physical self-regard that tip into something more searching.
In the Boffin household, surrounded by all that newly minted comfort, she studies her own reflection and the question underneath is always: who am I becoming?
The becoming is Dickens's real subject with Bella — not her arrival at virtue, but the process of discovering what she already was.
And what she discovers is that the woman she already was cannot survive inside the logic of wealth accumulation.
That is the novel's sharpest insight about Bella — and it rhymes with what it says about the dust heaps themselves.
The Harmon fortune is literally built on refuse — on what society throws away.
And the characters who are redeemed in this novel are precisely those who refuse to let that origin contaminate them.
Bella chooses love over legacy — and Dickens frames that choice as an act of seeing clearly, which is the only political act available to her within the novel's world.
What moves me most, finally, is the quality of happiness the novel extends to Bella at the end.
Dickens gives her a real domestic life — small, warm, slightly comic in its ordinariness.
She learns to keep house and laughs at herself doing it — there's that wonderful passage about her housekeeping experiments being, shall we say, imperfect.
And when she finally learns who John really is, her response is not triumph but a kind of awed, grateful simplicity.
She came to the novel's beginning as a young woman bequeated like furniture.
She ends it as a person who has chosen herself — which in Victorian fiction, for a woman, is genuinely radical.
Chosen herself — that's a beautiful place to rest for a moment.

What we've been tracing is a character who begins the novel as a kind of mirror held up to society's values — mercenary, clear-eyed, trapped — and who ends by seeing through the glass to something truer.
Eleanor, Daniel, Caroline — thank you for that.
When we return, we'll be moving to the river — to Lizzie Hexam and the world below the bridges, where the novel's other great feminine strength is forged in altogether darker water.

segments.title: Respectability and Rot: How the System Remakes Itself

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been circling the great dust heaps, the river, the money — and now we arrive at something that ties all of it together.
The question of respectability — what it costs, who it protects, and how the system uses it to reproduce itself endlessly.
Eleanor, you've written about Dickens as a novelist of surfaces — of how characters perform their social identities.
Where does that performance feel most dangerous in this novel?
The Veneerings are where I'd start — every time, without hesitation.
Dickens introduces them with one of the great satirical set-pieces in English fiction — that first dinner party in Book the First.
Everything about the Veneerings is new — the house, the furniture, the silver, the guests — because newness is the point.
Dickens writes that Mr. and Mrs. Veneering were bran-new people in a bran-new house in a bran-new quarter of London.
"Mr. and Mrs. Veneering were bran-new people in a bran-new house in a bran-new quarter of London."
The triple repetition is doing enormous structural work — it's comic, yes, but also quietly horrifying.
What Dickens is showing us is that respectability here has no history — it's manufactured on demand, like the furniture.
And the terrifying thing is that it works.
What Eleanor's identified is the novel's central economic insight, and I think it's even sharper than it first appears.
The Veneerings' social world isn't just a satire on social climbing — it's a portrait of how capitalism generates its own legitimacy.
Twemlow is the key figure here — the threadbare aristocrat who functions as the human standard of gentility at every one of these dinners.
He's wheeled out as a form of cultural capital — his ancient lineage launders the Veneerings' new money.
And then there's Podsnap — who I'd argue is the more disturbing figure because he has genuine conviction.
Dickens gives us the Podsnap Doctrine — the refusal to acknowledge anything that might bring a blush to the cheek of the Young Person.
That doctrine is the ideological machinery of respectability — it doesn't just ignore suffering, it enforces its own ignorance as a virtue.
Podsnap isn't hypocritical — he genuinely believes in the system he protects, which makes him far more dangerous than a mere fraud.
What strikes me as a reader is how Dickens makes you laugh at the Veneering world even as he's showing you something deeply bleak.
That mirror — the great looking-glass over the Veneering sideboard — is one of the most quietly brilliant devices in the book.
All the dinner guests are reflected in it, and Dickens describes them as if they're figures in a painting — fixed, posed, decorative.
He writes of the looking-glass reflecting the table and company — and the Analytical Chemist, the Veneerings' butler, lurking sorrowfully in the background.
The Analytical Chemist — that's what Dickens calls the butler — who regards the whole proceedings with professional contempt and existential gloom.
He's the only honest figure in the room, and he has no voice whatsoever.
Which is Dickens's point, isn't it — the people who see the performance most clearly are the ones the system makes invisible.
Caroline's right about visibility — and I want to connect that to what happens with Bella Wilfer and the Boffins.
The Boffins' sudden wealth is fascinating because Dickens uses it to test whether goodness can survive prosperity.
Mrs. Boffin instinctively reaches toward kindness — her campaign to adopt children named after those who died young is genuinely touching.
But Mr. Boffin performs the role of the miser as money corrupts him — or appears to — and Bella watches and is changed by it.
The novel is asking: what does watching wealth degrade someone do to your own desires?
And the structural sleight of hand — the revelation that Boffin has been performing the miser to educate Bella — is deeply ambivalent.
Because by then the performance has blurred with reality in ways Dickens never fully resolves.
The Boffin plot is one of the places where I think Dickens's radical instincts and his more conservative resolutions are genuinely in tension.
What the novel shows us with painful clarity is that there is no clean money in this world — every fortune has the dust heap behind it.
Old Harmon built his wealth on refuse — on what society throws away — and that's not incidental, it's the whole metaphor.
Society's waste generates wealth, and that wealth then purchases respectability, and respectability erases the origin of the wealth.
Silas Wegg sitting atop the dust mound, rifling through it for value — he's a grotesque mirror of how the whole system operates.
Everyone in this novel is scavenging — the question is only whether you do it with a ballad-sheet or a barrister's wig.
Daniel's line about the barrister's wig lands hard, because Dickens makes exactly that connection through Eugene Wrayburn.
Eugene is a barrister who does almost nothing — who performs the professional identity of respectable middle-class man with absolute cynicism.
His friendship with Mortimer Lightwood is one of the novel's great pleasures — witty, idle, elegantly despairing.
But what moves me is how Eugene is genuinely unsettled by Lizzie Hexam — she disturbs his comfortable irony.
She forces him to become, rather than simply to perform — and the novel treats that becoming as almost literally life-or-death.
The near-murder by Bradley Headstone isn't just melodrama — it's the moment when Eugene's ironic detachment from the world has consequences he can no longer aestheticize.
And his marriage to Lizzie in extremis — that's the system cracking open, however briefly.
The Bradley Headstone and Eugene dynamic is where Dickens does something genuinely unsettling with the idea of respectability.
Because Headstone is the self-made respectable man — the schoolmaster who has dragged himself up from nothing through sheer effort and discipline.
And Dickens describes that achievement as a kind of violence done to himself — the passion suppressed, the rough origin smoothed over.
Dickens writes that Headstone had acquired mechanically a great store of teacher's knowledge — but the acquisition sat uneasily.
The word mechanically is devastating — it tells you that the whole edifice of respectability has been built without interior conviction.
And then the passion for Lizzie tears all of it apart — the respectable surface simply cannot contain what's beneath it.
It's one of the most psychologically precise portraits of class anxiety in Victorian fiction.
Eleanor's reading of Headstone is exactly right, and I want to push it one step further.
Headstone is the novel's most devastating indictment of the Victorian ideology of self-improvement — the idea that effort and discipline can lift a man out of his origins.
He has done everything the system asked of him, and the system still treats him as lesser — Eugene Wrayburn, who has done nothing, still outranks him by birth.
The rage that produces the murder attempt — that's not a personal failing, that's a structural wound.
And Dickens is careful — Headstone is not sympathetic in any simple way, but his fury is legible, it has causes.
Rogue Riderhood's blackmail of Headstone and their shared drowning at the end — that's the system consuming its own casualties.
I keep coming back to Twemlow at the very end — the final scene at the dinner table, after Eugene and Lizzie's marriage becomes known.
Podsnap and the assembled company declare the marriage an outrage — a lady by somebody else's making marrying a mere bargeman's daughter.
And Twemlow — this mild, apparently ridiculous figure — stands up and quietly demolishes the whole room.
He says, in effect, that if Eugene is a gentleman and considered her a lady, that is a higher view of the case than any the room can offer.
Dickens writes that Twemlow put his hand to his forehead as if there were a slight ache there — and then said what he felt was true.
That gesture — the slight ache — is extraordinary. It carries decades of this mild man's suppressed conviction.
The novel ends on that note of quiet, stubborn, human decency — which makes it all the more fragile, and all the more precious.
Twemlow standing up — that image will stay with me.
What this conversation has traced is how respectability in Our Mutual Friend is never merely a social nicety — it's a mechanism of power, and the novel knows it.
The Veneerings' glittering surfaces, Headstone's mechanically acquired knowledge, Podsnap's enforced ignorance — all of it part of the same system.
And what the novel finds, in those moments of resistance — Twemlow's quiet courage, Lizzie's survival — is not a solution but a refusal.
After the break, we'll turn to the river — what it carries, what it takes, and what it returns.

segments.title: The Man From the River: Plot's Long Suspense

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart piece by piece — and put it back together with fresh eyes.
I'm your host, and today we are deep in the machinery of the novel's central mystery — what we might call the long suspense of John Harmon's fate.
With me are three guests who bring very different lenses to this remarkable book.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher obsessed with fictional architecture — she sees the skeleton inside every great sentence.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as maps of class power — and he will not let us forget what the Thames is actually carrying when it carries a body.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of classic fiction — she brings the experience of the page, the verbal music, the moments that make you stop breathing.
Today's segment is about plot and suspense — specifically, how Dickens withholds John Harmon's identity across hundreds of pages and what that withholding costs and creates.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — because this is, structurally, one of the strangest decisions in Victorian fiction.
It really is extraordinary when you stand back and look at what Dickens is doing with this plot.
The novel opens with a body being pulled from the Thames by Gaffer Hexam — that much is established immediately, with tremendous atmospheric force.

But the question of whose body it is — and whether the man we soon meet as Julius Handford, and then as John Rokesmith, is actually John Harmon — Dickens keeps that suspended for the better part of two volumes.
What I find technically fascinating is the chapter Dickens gives over entirely to Harmon's own interior reconstruction of events — the famous self-interrogation in Book Two.
He writes it in a fractured, doubling grammar — 'I could not have said then, and I cannot say now, that I am sure I was alive.'
'I could not have said then, and I cannot say now, that I am sure I was alive.'
That grammatical uncertainty — the tense doubling back on itself — is doing the work of trauma, of a consciousness that has been genuinely shattered and is rebuilding itself in real time.
No other Victorian novelist would hand an entire chapter to that kind of phenomenological puzzle and make it gripping.
I want to come at the same chapter from a different angle, because I think the content of what Harmon reconstructs is as important as the grammar.
What he slowly pieces together is that he was drugged, robbed, and very nearly murdered — by men operating in a criminal economy centred on the river.
The Thames in this novel is not picturesque — it is a labour site and a disposal site simultaneously.
Gaffer Hexam makes his living fishing out the dead — legally stripping them of valuables before he reports them.
Dickens gives him a ferocious opening line of self-justification — something to the effect that he has never turned a man face-downward in the water, he only finds what the river gives him.
'I do not,
That self-exculpation is the moral grammar of the entire novel's economic world — everyone at every level insists their hands are clean because they only profit from what was already there.
The dust heaps, the inheritance, the marriage market for Bella Wilfer — it is all the same structure.
What strikes me, reading this opening movement again, is how purely physical Dickens makes the suspense feel.
That first chapter on the river — the dark water, the boat, Gaffer and Lizzie — it has almost no plot information at all.
But Dickens charges every sensation: the way the oars move, the way Lizzie refuses to look at what her father is towing.
Lizzie's averted face in that opening chapter is one of the great pieces of body language in the Victorian novel, I think.
She can't look — not because she doesn't know, but because she knows too well and has decided that knowing costs something.
And that is the emotional register the whole mystery runs on — not dramatic irony exactly, but a kind of shared, unspoken dread between characters and reader.
Caroline, you've put your finger on something I find structurally brilliant — Dickens is running two separate suspense engines simultaneously.
There is the external mystery: whose body is it, is Harmon alive, who is Rokesmith really?
And there is the internal, almost existential question that the Harmon chapter makes explicit — can a man who has been so thoroughly unmade reconstitute himself as a person?
He speaks of watching himself from the outside, of being able to follow his own movements as though he were a stranger.
'I mentally pursued the investigation, as if the subject were another man.'
That dissociative grammar is the formal enactment of identity loss — the plot's mystery and the character's psychology are the exact same thing.
And here I'd push on what that identity loss is actually constituted by — because it's not random.
Harmon has been shaped, or rather deformed, by his father's will — the inheritance, the demand that he marry a woman he has never met as the price of receiving a fortune built on filth.
So his identity crisis is not merely personal — it is the novel's most concentrated image of what inherited wealth does to a human being.
His father tried to purchase him a life from beyond the grave, and the violence that nearly kills him is just the most literal version of what that inheritance is always doing.
The disguise as Rokesmith — working as secretary in the Boffin household — is his attempt to earn a self the market hasn't already bought.
That's what makes the Bella Wilfer plot so unexpectedly moving, for me at least.
She starts the novel as a character who knows her own price — she's quite honest about it, almost brutally so.
She says she is 'a very vain, silly, mercenary little creature' — which is Dickens giving her the most self-aware line of self-condemnation you could imagine.
'A very vain, silly, mercenary little creature.'
And what Rokesmith — Harmon — does is refuse to confirm that verdict by treating her as though she is already something better.
Their courtship under false names is quietly the most romantic thing in the novel — two people constructing each other outside the machinery of the plot.
That phrase — 'outside the machinery' — feels like exactly the right description of what Dickens is after with this long deception.
The plot withholds, but that withholding creates a sheltered space where something more genuine can happen.
In our next segment we'll follow that machinery into darker water — into Rogue Riderhood, Bradley Headstone, and the novel's second great arc of violence and obsession.
We've spent this episode deep inside the novel's machinery — its rivers and dust-heaps, its frauds and its tenderness.
Before we close, I want to ask each of you a version of the same question.
What did Dickens know — about us, about society, about the human animal — that we still haven't fully reckoned with?
What strikes me most, closing the novel, is how clearly Dickens understood that identity is a performance — and that the performance can swallow the performer.
Think of John Harmon — he spends the entire novel disguised as John Rokesmith, and the disguise becomes almost more real than the man underneath.
Dickens gives him that extraordinary soliloquy in Book Two — 'I have no name. I had no name.'
'I, the real John Harmon, I am as dead as if I had never been.'
That's not melodrama — that's a precise psychological observation about what sustained deception costs a person.
Dickens knew, a hundred and sixty years ago, that the self is not a fixed thing — it's something you can lose.
I'd put it slightly differently — though I don't disagree with Eleanor at all.
What Dickens knew is that money doesn't just buy things — it rewrites people's moral grammar.
Look at the Veneerings — their entire social existence is fabricated from wealth so new it barely has time to cool.
Dickens describes their dinner table as 'the Veneering establishment' — and the word 'establishment' does so much work.
It's an institution before it's a home — a place for the transaction of social credit.
And the guests at that table — Twemlow, Lady Tippins, all of them — they're not friends, they're instruments.
What Dickens saw — and what we still haven't fully confronted — is that capitalism doesn't corrupt society from outside.
It is society, when society is organised around the pursuit of money above everything else.
Both of those feel true to me — and they converge, I think, in the novel's most quietly devastating character.
Not Harmon, not the Veneerings — Betty Higden.
An old woman who would rather die on the road than enter the workhouse — and who does die, essentially, on that principle.
Dickens gives her a speech that is almost unbearable to read — she talks about the Poor Law as a thing that hunts her.
'I have fought against the parish and fled from it, and there is no help for it, and it will be upon me when I am past help.'
She's not a victim waiting for rescue — she has fierce, exhausted dignity.
And what Dickens knew is that dignity and destitution can coexist — and that society's cruelty consists partly in refusing to see that.
Caroline's point about Betty Higden makes me think about craft again — because Dickens earns that moment technically.
He doesn't sentimentalise her death — he surrounds it with the beauty of the English countryside, and that contrast is deliberate and brutal.
The novel as a whole does that — it holds beauty and ugliness in the same frame, almost without comment.
The river gives up the dead and the living in the same gesture — Gaffer Hexam's livelihood is also London's open sewer.
Dickens knew that the novel form could hold that doubleness — could make you laugh at the Veneerings and weep for Betty Higden in the same afternoon's reading.
That tonal range is what makes it not just a great Victorian novel but a living one.
And I'd add — the ending doesn't entirely redeem the world it has described.
Harmon gets his money, Bella becomes genuinely good, Lizzie Hexam gets Eugene Wrayburn — happy endings, of a kind.
But Twemlow's final speech — defending Lizzie's marriage against Lady Tippins's social snobbery — is remarkable precisely because it solves nothing.
One decent man says a decent thing at a dinner table — and goes home alone.
Dickens gives Twemlow the last moral word, and then quietly puts him back in his chambers in Duke Street, alone with his folding bedstead.
That is a writer who knows that moral courage and social power are not the same thing.
Twemlow always gets me — he's so easy to underestimate, and then suddenly he's the spine of the whole novel.
And I think that's one more thing Dickens knew — that goodness doesn't announce itself loudly.
It lives in people who fold up their beds and go back to their small lives and still tell the truth when asked.
Riah, Jenny Wren, Mr. Boffin pretending to be monstrous in order to protect Bella — the whole novel is full of people doing good quietly and at cost.
I keep coming back to the title — Our Mutual Friend.
It's how the Boffins and the Wilfers are connected to the Harmon estate — through John Harmon himself, who no one quite knows.
But Dickens makes it feel larger than that — as if we are all each other's mutual friends, whether we acknowledge it or not.
That feels like exactly the right place to close — with the title as a kind of quiet ethical claim about human connection.
Eleanor, Daniel, Caroline — it has been a genuine pleasure thinking through this novel with you.
Our Mutual Friend rewards every reading — and this conversation has reminded me why.
For listeners joining us for the first time — go back to the beginning of this episode, and then go read the novel.
This has been Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Thank you for listening.

The state of the man was murderous, and he knew it. More; he irritated it,
      with a kind of perverse pleasure akin to that which a sick man sometimes
      has in irritating a wound upon his body. Tied up all day with his
      disciplined show upon him, subdued to the performance of his routine of
      educational tricks, encircled by a gabbling crowd, he broke loose at night
      like an ill-tamed wild animal. Under his daily restraint, it was his
      compensation, not his trouble, to give a glance towards his state at
      night, and to the freedom of its being indulged. If great criminals told
      the truth—which, being great criminals, they do not—they would
      very rarely tell of their struggles against the crime. Their struggles are
      towards it. They buffet with opposing waves, to gain the bloody shore, not
      to recede from it. This man perfectly comprehended that he hated his rival
      with his strongest and worst forces, and that if he tracked him to Lizzie
      Hexam, his so doing would never serve himself with her, or serve her. All
      his pains were taken, to the end that he might incense himself with the
      sight of the detested figure in her company and favour, in her place of
      concealment. And he knew as well what act of his would follow if he did,
      as he knew that his mother had borne him. Granted, that he may not have
      held it necessary to make express mention to himself of the one familiar
      truth any more than of the other.
c44:p1.summary: Bradley consciously cultivates his murderous hatred, finding perverse pleasure in his rage. Dickens digresses to philosophize on the nature of great criminals: they struggle toward crime, not against it. Bradley fully understands his hatred and its inevitable consequences.

‘I had drank some coffee, when to my sense of sight he began to swell
      immensely, and something urged me to rush at him. We had a struggle near
      the door. He got from me, through my not knowing where to strike, in the
      whirling round of the room, and the flashing of flames of fire between us.
      I dropped down. Lying helpless on the ground, I was turned over by a foot.
      I was dragged by the neck into a corner. I heard men speak together. I was
      turned over by other feet. I saw a figure like myself lying dressed in my
      clothes on a bed. What might have been, for anything I knew, a silence of
      days, weeks, months, years, was broken by a violent wrestling of men all
      over the room. The figure like myself was assailed, and my valise was in
      its hand. I was trodden upon and fallen over. I heard a noise of blows,
      and thought it was a wood-cutter cutting down a tree. I could not have
      said that my name was John Harmon—I could not have thought it—I
      didn’t know it—but when I heard the blows, I thought of the
      wood-cutter and his axe, and had some dead idea that I was lying in a
      forest.

‘’Scuse  me , Lawyer Lightwood, it’s a part of the truth, and as such I do
      mind it, and I must mind it and I will mind it. “Rogue Riderhood,” he
      says, “words passed betwixt us on the river tonight.” Which they had; ask

      with my boat’s stretcher, or take a aim at your brains with my boathook. I
      did so on accounts of your looking too hard at what I had in tow, as if
      you was suspicious, and on accounts of your holding on to the gunwale of
      my boat.” I says to him, “Gaffer, I know it.” He says to me, “Rogue
      Riderhood, you are a man in a dozen”—I think he said in a score, but
      of that I am not positive, so take the lowest figure, for precious be the
      obligations of a Alfred David. “And,” he says, “when your fellow-men is
      up, be it their lives or be it their watches, sharp is ever the word with
      you. Had you suspicions?” I says, “Gaffer, I had; and what’s more, I
      have.” He falls a shaking, and he says, “Of what?” I says, “Of foul play.”
       He falls a shaking worse, and he says, “There  was  foul play then. I done
      it for his money. Don’t betray me!” Those were the words as ever he used.’

‘No I don’t,’ said the little creature, resting one arm upon the elbow of
      her chair, resting her chin upon that hand, and looking vacantly before
      her; ‘this is not a flowery neighbourhood. It’s anything but that. And yet
      as I sit at work, I smell miles of flowers. I smell roses, till I think I

      leaves, till I put down my hand—so—and expect to make them
      rustle. I smell the white and the pink May in the hedges, and all sorts of
      flowers that I never was among. For I have seen very few flowers indeed,

c33:p97.text:
‘Tell him I am a match-maker; tell him I am an artful and designing woman;
      tell him you are sure his daughter is best out of my house and my company.
      Tell him any such things of me; they will all be true. You know what a
      puffed-up man he is, and how easily you can cause his vanity to take the
      alarm. Tell him as much as will give him the alarm and make him careful of
      her, and spare me the rest. Mr Twemlow, I feel my sudden degradation in
      your eyes; familiar as I am with my degradation in my own eyes, I keenly
      feel the change that must have come upon me in yours, in these last few
      moments. But I trust to your good faith with me as implicitly as when I
      began. If you knew how often I have tried to speak to you to-day, you
      would almost pity me. I want no new promise from you on my own account,
      for I am satisfied, and I always shall be satisfied, with the promise you
      have given me. I can venture to say no more, for I see that I am watched.
      If you would set my mind at rest with the assurance that you will
      interpose with the father and save this harmless girl, close that book
      before you return it to me, and I shall know what you mean, and deeply
      thank you in my heart.—Alfred, Mr Twemlow thinks the last one the
      best, and quite agrees with you and me.’

Strictly speaking, it would be hard to show cause why they should not
      bring him in, Pocket-Breaches having closed its little bargain, and there
      being no opposition. However, it is agreed that they must ‘work’ to the
      last, and that if they did not work, something indefinite would happen. It
      is likewise agreed that they are all so exhausted with the work behind
      them, and need to be so fortified for the work before them, as to require
      peculiar strengthening from Veneering’s cellar. Therefore, the Analytical
      has orders to produce the cream of the cream of his binns, and therefore
      it falls out that rallying becomes rather a trying word for the occasion;
      Lady Tippins being observed gamely to inculcate the necessity of rearing
      round their dear Veneering; Podsnap advocating roaring round him; Boots
      and Brewer declaring their intention of reeling round him; and Veneering
      thanking his devoted friends one and all, with great emotion, for
      rarullarulling round him.

c33:p48.text:
However, the great subject of the happiness of Mr and Mrs Lammle must not
      be allowed to vanish with the other vanishments—with the vanishing
      of the murderer, the vanishing of Julius Handford, the vanishing of Lizzie
      Hexam,—and therefore Veneering must recall the present sheep to the
      pen from which they have strayed. Who so fit to discourse of the happiness
      of Mr and Mrs Lammle, they being the dearest and oldest friends he has in
      the world; or what audience so fit for him to take into his confidence as
      that audience, a noun of multitude or signifying many, who are all the
      oldest and dearest friends he has in the world? So Veneering, without the
      formality of rising, launches into a familiar oration, gradually toning
      into the Parliamentary sing-song, in which he sees at that board his dear
      friend Twemlow who on that day twelvemonth bestowed on his dear friend
      Lammle the fair hand of his dear friend Sophronia, and in which he also
      sees at that board his dear friends Boots and Brewer whose rallying round
      him at a period when his dear friend Lady Tippins likewise rallied round
      him—ay, and in the foremost rank—he can never forget while
      memory holds her seat. But he is free to confess that he misses from that
      board his dear old friend Podsnap, though he is well represented by his
      dear young friend Georgiana. And he further sees at that board (this he
      announces with pomp, as if exulting in the powers of an extraordinary
      telescope) his friend Mr Fledgeby, if he will permit him to call him so.
      For all of these reasons, and many more which he right well knows will
      have occurred to persons of your exceptional acuteness, he is here to
      submit to you that the time has arrived when, with our hearts in our
      glasses, with tears in our eyes, with blessings on our lips, and in a
      general way with a profusion of gammon and spinach in our emotional
      larders, we should one and all drink to our dear friends the Lammles,
      wishing them many years as happy as the last, and many many friends as
      congenially united as themselves. And this he will add; that Anastatia
      Veneering (who is instantly heard to weep) is formed on the same model as
      her old and chosen friend Sophronia Lammle, in respect that she is devoted
      to the man who wooed and won her, and nobly discharges the duties of a
      wife.
c33:p48.summary: Veneering delivers an extended, self-congratulatory oration celebrating the Lammles' marriage and the assembled company's friendship, filled with parliamentary bombast and hypocritical sentiment.
c33:p48.best_quote: a profusion of gammon and spinach in our emotional larders

c20:p51.text:
‘My love,’ says Lady Tippins, ‘compose yourself; we’ll bring him in.’ And
      Lady Tippins really does work, and work the Veneering horses too; for she
      clatters about town all day, calling upon everybody she knows, and showing
      her entertaining powers and green fan to immense advantage, by rattling on
      with, My dear soul, what do you think? What do you suppose me to be?
      You’ll never guess. I’m pretending to be an electioneering agent. And for
      what place of all places? Pocket-Breaches. And why? Because the dearest
      friend I have in the world has bought it. And who is the dearest friend I
      have in the world? A man of the name of Veneering. Not omitting his wife,
      who is the other dearest friend I have in the world; and I positively
      declare I forgot their baby, who is the other. And we are carrying on this
      little farce to keep up appearances, and isn’t it refreshing! Then, my
      precious child, the fun of it is that nobody knows who these Veneerings
      are, and that they know nobody, and that they have a house out of the
      Tales of the Genii, and give dinners out of the Arabian Nights. Curious to
      see ’em, my dear? Say you’ll know ’em. Come and dine with ’em. They shan’t
      bore you. Say who shall meet you. We’ll make up a party of our own, and
      I’ll engage that they shall not interfere with you for one single moment.
      You really ought to see their gold and silver camels. I call their
      dinner-table, the Caravan. Do come and dine with my Veneerings, my own
      Veneerings, my exclusive property, the dearest friends I have in the
      world! And above all, my dear, be sure you promise me your vote and
      interest and all sorts of plumpers for Pocket-Breaches; for we couldn’t
      think of spending sixpence on it, my love, and can only consent to be
      brought in by the spontaneous thingummies of the incorruptible
      whatdoyoucallums.

c33:p6.text:
And dear Mrs Lammle and dear Mr Lammle, how do you do, and when are you
      going down to what’s-its-name place—Guy, Earl of Warwick, you know—what
      is it?—Dun Cow—to claim the flitch of bacon? And Mortimer,
      whose name is for ever blotted out from my list of lovers, by reason first
      of fickleness and then of base desertion, how do  you  do, wretch? And Mr
      Wrayburn,  you  here! What can  you  come for, because we are all very sure
      before-hand that you are not going to talk! And Veneering, M.P., how are
      things going on down at the house, and when will you turn out those
      terrible people for us? And Mrs Veneering, my dear, can it positively be
      true that you go down to that stifling place night after night, to hear
      those men prose? Talking of which, Veneering, why don’t you prose, for you
      haven’t opened your lips there yet, and we are dying to hear what you have
      got to say to us! Miss Podsnap, charmed to see you. Pa, here? No! Ma,
      neither? Oh! Mr Boots! Delighted. Mr Brewer! This  is  a gathering of the
      clans. Thus Tippins, and surveys Fledgeby and outsiders through golden
      glass, murmuring as she turns about and about, in her innocent giddy way,
      Anybody else I know? No, I think not. Nobody there. Nobody  there . Nobody
      anywhere!

c67:p57.text:
When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.

c67:p58.text:
To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out,
      another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a
      pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and
      the most difficult part of my design. Its difficulty was much enhanced by
      the mode of publication; for, it would be very unreasonable to expect that
      many readers, pursuing a story in portions from month to month through
      nineteen months, will, until they have it before them complete, perceive
      the relations of its finer threads to the whole pattern which is always
      before the eyes of the story-weaver at his loom. Yet, that I hold the
      advantages of the mode of publication to outweigh its disadvantages, may
      be easily believed of one who revived it in the Pickwick Papers after long
      disuse, and has pursued it ever since.
c67:p58.summary: Dickens reflects on the difficulty of maintaining a secret subplot across serialized publication, defending the mode of publication despite its challenges.

c67:p60.text:
In my social experiences since Mrs Betty Higden came upon the scene and
      left it, I have found Circumlocutional champions disposed to be warm with
      me on the subject of my view of the Poor Law. My friend Mr Bounderby could
      never see any difference between leaving the Coketown ‘hands’ exactly as
      they were, and requiring them to be fed with turtle soup and venison out
      of gold spoons. Idiotic propositions of a parallel nature have been freely
      offered for my acceptance, and I have been called upon to admit that I
      would give Poor Law relief to anybody, anywhere, anyhow. Putting this
      nonsense aside, I have observed a suspicious tendency in the champions to
      divide into two parties; the one, contending that there are no deserving
      Poor who prefer death by slow starvation and bitter weather, to the
      mercies of some Relieving Officers and some Union Houses; the other,
      admitting that there are such Poor, but denying that they have any cause
      or reason for what they do. The records in our newspapers, the late
      exposure by  The Lancet , and the common sense and senses of common people,
      furnish too abundant evidence against both defences. But, that my view of
      the Poor Law may not be mistaken or misrepresented, I will state it. I
      believe there has been in England, since the days of the  Stuarts , no law
      so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law
      habitually so ill-supervised. In the majority of the shameful cases of
      disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the
      country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known
      language could say no more of their lawlessness.

‘The reference,’ proceeds Mortimer, ‘which I suppose to be made by my
      honourable and fair enslaver opposite, is to the following circumstance.
      Very lately, the young woman, Lizzie Hexam, daughter of the late Jesse
      Hexam, otherwise Gaffer, who will be remembered to have found the body of
      the man from somewhere, mysteriously received, she knew not from whom, an
      explicit retraction of the charges made against her father, by another
      water-side character of the name of Riderhood. Nobody believed them,
      because little Rogue Riderhood—I am tempted into the paraphrase by
      remembering the charming wolf who would have rendered society a great
      service if he had devoured Mr Riderhood’s father and mother in their
      infancy—had previously played fast and loose with the said charges,
      and, in fact, abandoned them. However, the retraction I have mentioned
      found its way into Lizzie Hexam’s hands, with a general flavour on it of
      having been favoured by some anonymous messenger in a dark cloak and
      slouched hat, and was by her forwarded, in her father’s vindication, to Mr
      Boffin, my client. You will excuse the phraseology of the shop, but as I
      never had another client, and in all likelihood never shall have, I am
      rather proud of him as a natural curiosity probably unique.’

c67:p61.text:
On Friday the Ninth of June in the present year, Mr and Mrs Boffin (in
      their manuscript dress of receiving Mr and Mrs Lammle at breakfast) were
      on the South Eastern Railway with me, in a terribly destructive accident.
      When I had done what I could to help others, I climbed back into my
      carriage—nearly turned over a viaduct, and caught aslant upon the
      turn—to extricate the worthy couple. They were much soiled, but
      otherwise unhurt. The same happy result attended Miss Bella Wilfer on her
      wedding day, and Mr Riderhood inspecting Bradley Headstone’s red
      neckerchief as he lay asleep. I remember with devout thankfulness that I
      can never be much nearer parting company with my readers for ever, than I
      was then, until there shall be written against my life, the two words with
      which I have this day closed this book:—THE END.
c67:p61.summary: Dickens recounts his experience in the Staplehurst railway accident of June 9, 1865, expressing gratitude for his miraculous escape and reflecting on mortality in connection with the novel's conclusion.

c2:p3.text:
But, it was not this which steeped the feeble soul of Twemlow in
      confusion. This he was used to, and could take soundings of. The abyss to
      which he could find no bottom, and from which started forth the engrossing
      and ever-swelling difficulty of his life, was the insoluble question
      whether he was Veneering’s oldest friend, or newest friend. To the
      excogitation of this problem, the harmless gentleman had devoted many
      anxious hours, both in his lodgings over the livery stable-yard, and in
      the cold gloom, favourable to meditation, of Saint James’s Square. Thus.
      Twemlow had first known Veneering at his club, where Veneering then knew
      nobody but the man who made them known to one another, who seemed to be
      the most intimate friend he had in the world, and whom he had known two
      days—the bond of union between their souls, the nefarious conduct of
      the committee respecting the cookery of a fillet of veal, having been
      accidentally cemented at that date. Immediately upon this, Twemlow
      received an invitation to dine with Veneering, and dined: the man being of
      the party. Immediately upon that, Twemlow received an invitation to dine
      with the man, and dined: Veneering being of the party. At the man’s were a
      Member, an Engineer, a Payer-off of the National Debt, a Poem on
      Shakespeare, a Grievance, and a Public Office, who all seem to be utter
      strangers to Veneering. And yet immediately after that, Twemlow received
      an invitation to dine at Veneerings, expressly to meet the Member, the
      Engineer, the Payer-off of the National Debt, the Poem on Shakespeare, the
      Grievance, and the Public Office, and, dining, discovered that all of them
      were the most intimate friends Veneering had in the world, and that the
      wives of all of them (who were all there) were the objects of Mrs
      Veneering’s most devoted affection and tender confidence.
c2:p3.summary: Twemlow recounts his baffling experience of being introduced to Veneering, noting how Veneering's friends constantly shift and how he cannot determine his own position in the social hierarchy.
c2:p3.best_quote: the insoluble question whether he was Veneering's oldest friend, or newest friend
